plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two fragments of a recursion tree side by side, labeled (a) and (b), with nodes carrying subproblem sizes. In (a) a top node labeled n has two branches: the left ends at a bare 0 with no box drawn around it, the right at a node labeled n-1. A large pale gray ellipse encloses the top node and the n-1 node together, and a heavy dotted arrow runs from that ellipse rightward to the expression Theta(n). The n-1 node branches in turn to two gray rectangles reading (n-1)/2 - 1 and (n-1)/2. In (b) a single node labeled n is ringed by a small pale gray ellipse, again with a dotted arrow pointing right to Theta(n), and it branches to two gray rectangles that both read (n-1)/2. The shared Theta(n) tag is the point of the comparison: the shaded groupings cost the same in each panel, while the boxed subproblems still waiting differ. Putting a lopsided split followed by an even one beside a single even split motivates the argument that alternating bad and good partitions costs about what uninterrupted good partitioning would.

interactions.label: Split pattern
interactions.teaches: The shaded Θ(n) cost group is comparable in both fragments even though the leftover subproblem boxes differ — a bad split plus a good split leaves roughly the same total work waiting as one good split

interactions.label: Expand next level
interactions.teaches: Each expansion reveals the children the current split produces and updates the accumulated cost, showing how partition balance controls the width and depth of the recursion tree
Clicking the shaded ellipse brightens exactly the nodes whose partitioning work is being counted as one Θ(n) level, clarifying which work the dotted arrow is summing

demo_steps.title: Balanced split
demo_steps.narration: In the balanced fragment, node n splits evenly into two (n−1)/2 boxes; the small ellipse around n alone is tagged Θ(n), the cost of this one partitioning step.

demo_steps.title: Alternating bad–good split
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the alternating fragment: n first splits lopsidedly into 0 and n−1, and the large ellipse groups n with n−1 — yet it is still tagged Θ(n), the same per-level cost as the balanced case.

demo_steps.title: Expand the good split
demo_steps.narration: Expanding one more level shows n−1 splitting evenly into (n−1)/2 − 1 and (n−1)/2; the bad split's waste is recovered by the following good split, so the leftover boxes match the balanced fragment's and the level cost stays Θ(n).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A lopsided partition's extra cost is absorbed by the next even partition, so alternating bad and good splits keeps each level's work at Θ(n) — the same as uninterrupted balanced partitioning.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out two side-by-side tree fragments on a white background, captions (a) and (b) centered beneath each. Use serif italic math styling for n, n−1, (n−1)/2, (n−1)/2 − 1 and Θ(n). In (a) draw the top node n with a left edge to a bare '0' (no rectangle) and a right edge to node n−1; enclose n and n−1 in one large pale-gray rotated ellipse and run a thick dotted arrow from it to Θ(n) on the right; below n−1 draw two gray-filled rectangles (n−1)/2 − 1 and (n−1)/2. In (b) draw node n inside a small pale-gray ellipse with a dotted arrow to Θ(n), and two gray rectangles both reading (n−1)/2 below it. Keep ellipse fill light gray (~15% opacity) so the brighten-on-click highlight is clearly visible; gray rectangles a slightly darker neutral fill. Edges thin solid black. The dotted cost arrows and Θ(n) tags should align horizontally across the two panels to invite direct comparison.

authoredContext:
In the average case, PARTITION produces a mix of “good” and “bad” splits. In a recursion tree for an average-case execution of PARTITION, the good and bad splits are distributed randomly throughout the tree. Suppose, for the sake of intuition, that the good and bad splits alternate levels in the tree, and that the good splits are best-case splits and the bad splits are worst-case splits. Figure 7.5(a) shows the splits at two consecutive levels in the recursion tree. At the root of the tree, the cost is n for partitioning, and the subarrays produced have sizes n 1 and 0: the worst case. At the next level, the subarray of size n 1 undergoes best-case partitioning into subarrays of size .n 1/=2 1 and .n 1/=2. Let’s assume that the boundary-condition cost is 1 for the subarray of size 0. The combination of the bad split followed by the good split produces three subarrays of sizes 0, .n  1/=2  1, and .n  1/=2 at a combined partitioning cost
of ‚.n/ C ‚.n  1/ D ‚.n/. Certainly, this situation is no worse than that in
Figure 7.5(b), namely a single level of partitioning that produces two subarrays of
size .n  1/=2, at a cost of ‚.n/. Yet this latter situation is balanced! Intuitively,
the ‚.n  1/ cost of the bad split can be absorbed into the ‚.n/ cost of the good
split, and the resulting split is good. Thus, the running time of quicksort, when levels alternate between good and bad splits, is like the running time for good splits
alone: still O.n lg n/, but with a slightly larger constant hidden by the O-notation.
We shall give a rigorous analysis of the expected running time of a randomized
version of quicksort in Section 7.4.2.

discrepancies: The two gray boxes in panel (a) — '(n−1)/2 − 1' and '(n−1)/2' — slightly overlap (right edge of first at x=279, left edge of second at x=276) whereas the source shows a clear gap between them
The gray ellipse in panel (a) appears slightly smaller and less prominent than in the source, where it more boldly encompasses both n and n−1
The dotted arrow in the source uses thicker, more widely-spaced dots; the generated version's dasharray '0.5,8' produces finer dots that read slightly differently at a glance
evaluation.notes: The figure faithfully reproduces both panels with correct tree topology, node labels, gray shading, ellipses, and Θ(n) cost arrows; interactions (step player, expand/collapse, split-pattern highlighting) are meaningful and pedagogically sound, with only minor geometric issues like the overlapping boxes in panel (a).
